subject: biology

items.q: Which statement about the organisms that cause infectious diseases in humans is correct?
items.correct: Viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists all include species that are human pathogens, but archaea are not known to be.
items.misconception: Only bacteria and viruses cause infectious diseases in humans; fungi and protists do not cause any.
items.why: The infectious diseases most often used as examples in earlier courses (tuberculosis, cholera, measles, influenza) are bacterial or viral, so the two groups become the whole category in students' minds. A broad range of disease-causing organisms can infect humans. Fungi (for example the cause of athlete's foot and of the pneumonia seen in AIDS) and protists (for example the cause of malaria) are pathogens as much as bacteria and viruses are.
items.specStatementText: Pathogens cause infectious disease, and observation beat germ theory to it
items.random_wrong: Archaea, like bacteria, include many species that are human pathogens, because both groups are prokaryotes.

items.q: In 1854 John Snow recorded the addresses of people who died of cholera in Soho, London, and found that the deaths clustered around one public water pump. The pump handle was removed and the outbreak subsided. At that time the germ theory of disease had not been established. What does this episode illustrate about how science makes progress?
items.correct: Careful observation of a pattern in the data can lead to effective control of a disease before its cause is known.
items.misconception: A disease can be controlled only once the microorganism that causes it has been identified in the laboratory.
items.why: Germ theory is taught as the foundation of modern medicine, so students assume that explanation must always come before effective action and that observation without a mechanism cannot justify a change in practice. Careful observation can lead to important progress. Semmelweis's hand-washing and the removal of the Broad Street pump handle both reduced deaths before anyone knew that bacteria caused the diseases; the pattern in the data was enough to act on.
items.specStatementText: Pathogens cause infectious disease, and observation beat germ theory to it
items.random_wrong: Once Snow's conclusion had been published, it was certain and did not need to be evaluated by other scientists.

items.q: Sebaceous glands in the skin secrete sebum. Which statement explains how sebum contributes to the skin's role as a primary defence against pathogens?
items.correct: It makes the skin surface a chemical barrier: its fatty acids keep the pH low, inhibiting the growth of many pathogens.
items.misconception: It thickens the dead outer layer of the skin, so that the physical barrier becomes much harder for pathogens to penetrate.
items.why: Earlier courses list the skin under 'physical barriers' and give stomach acid as the chemical example, so the chemical role of the skin's own secretions is not met. The skin acts as both a physical and a chemical barrier to pathogens. Sebum from sebaceous glands contains fatty acids that lower the pH of the skin surface, which inhibits the growth of many pathogens.
items.specStatementText: Skin and mucous membranes stop pathogens getting in
items.random_wrong: It carries antibodies out onto the skin surface, where they bind to any pathogens before these can penetrate into the skin.

items.q: Which sequence correctly describes the events that seal a cut in the skin?
items.correct: Platelets release clotting factors; a cascade produces thrombin; thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin; fibrin traps erythrocytes.
items.misconception: Platelets release clotting factors; a cascade produces thrombin; thrombin converts fibrin to fibrinogen; fibrinogen then traps erythrocytes.
items.why: The two names are similar and both are met at the same time, and students know that blood 'contains what it needs to clot', so the insoluble end product is assumed to be the circulating form. Fibrinogen is the soluble form that circulates; thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, which is insoluble and forms the mesh. If fibrin were present all the time, the blood would clot inside intact vessels.
items.specStatementText: Clotting seals a cut
items.random_wrong: Platelets stick to each other and to the edges of the cut, forming a solid plug that is itself the clot; no plasma proteins are involved at all.

items.q: Fibrinogen circulates in the plasma of healthy people all the time, yet clots form only where a blood vessel has been damaged. Which statement best explains this?
items.correct: Thrombin, the enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, is produced by a cascade that starts only when platelets release clotting factors at a site of damage.
items.misconception: Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin only when it is exposed to the air at an open wound, so a clot cannot form inside a vessel that is intact.
items.why: Blood that has leaked out is seen to dry and harden in the air, and students have no other everyday experience of clotting. Clotting is triggered by damage, not by air: platelets at the damaged site release clotting factors, and the cascade that follows produces thrombin. Clots form in the same way inside the body, for example in a bruise or a thrombosis, with no air present.
items.specStatementText: Clotting seals a cut
items.random_wrong: Fibrin is already present in the plasma, but its threads only become tangled into a mesh where the flow of blood is disturbed by damage.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the innate immune system from the adaptive immune system?
items.correct: The innate system responds to broad categories of pathogen and does not change during life; the adaptive system is specific and builds a memory of pathogens.
items.misconception: Both systems build up a memory of the pathogens they meet, but the innate system does so faster because it does not need to be specific to each one.
items.why: The everyday idea of 'building up immunity' is applied to the whole immune system, and phagocytes are the immune cells students know best, so they are credited with the improvement. The innate system, including phagocytes, responds in the same way every time. It is the adaptive system that responds in a specific way to particular pathogens and builds up a memory, so the immune response becomes more effective.
items.specStatementText: Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
items.random_wrong: The innate system is the specific one, with each phagocyte recognizing just a single type of pathogen, while the lymphocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen.

items.q: A person is infected by the same strain of a virus twice, two years apart. The second time, the number of virus particles in the blood peaks at a much lower level and falls to zero in half the time. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The adaptive immune system had retained a memory of the virus, so its specific response was faster and more effective the second time.
items.misconception: Antibodies made during the first infection had stayed in the blood at their peak concentration for two years and destroyed the virus at once.
items.why: Antibodies are what blood tests measure and what vaccines are said to produce, so antibodies come to stand for protection itself. Immunity is due to the long-term survival of lymphocytes that are capable of making the specific antibodies needed. These are memory cells; antibodies are proteins that are broken down over months.
items.specStatementText: Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
items.random_wrong: Phagocytes of the innate immune system had learned to recognize this virus during the first infection, so they engulfed it faster the second time.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium?
items.correct: It engulfs the bacterium by endocytosis and then digests it inside the cell, using the enzymes from its lysosomes.
items.misconception: It secretes enzymes from its lysosomes onto the bacterium, digesting it outside the cell, and then absorbs the soluble products.
items.why: External digestion is the pattern students know from fungi and from the gut, and it seems safer for the cell than taking a pathogen inside. Phagocytes engulf pathogens by endocytosis and digest them using enzymes from lysosomes, which fuse with the vesicle containing the pathogen. Digestion is intracellular.
items.specStatementText: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens
items.random_wrong: It lets the bacterium pass straight through its plasma membrane into the cytoplasm, where cytoplasmic enzymes break it down.

items.q: A splinter carrying bacteria lodges in the connective tissue of a finger, some distance from the nearest capillary. Within hours the bacteria are being destroyed by phagocytes. Which statement describes how this happens?
items.correct: Phagocytes leave the capillary by amoeboid movement, crawl through the tissue to the bacteria, then engulf them by endocytosis and digest them.
items.misconception: Phagocytes remain inside the capillary; tissue fluid carries the bacteria into the blood, where the phagocytes engulf and digest them.
items.why: Phagocytes are introduced as 'white blood cells', and blood cells are pictured as confined to vessels like erythrocytes. Phagocytes use amoeboid movement to pass from the blood to sites of infection in tissues, where they recognize and engulf pathogens.
items.specStatementText: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens
items.random_wrong: Phagocytes in the capillary secrete lysosomal enzymes into the tissue fluid, which diffuse to the splinter and digest the bacteria there.

items.q: Which statement about B-lymphocytes and antibodies is correct?
items.correct: A person has a very large number of different B-lymphocytes, and each of them makes a single specific type of antibody.
items.misconception: Each B-lymphocyte examines the antigen it meets and then adjusts the shape of the antibody it makes so that it fits the antigen.
items.why: The words 'adaptive' and 'specific response' suggest tailoring, and the lock-and-key fit of antibody to antigen is met after the antigen, as if the antigen came first. An individual has a very large number of B-lymphocytes that each make a specific type of antibody. The antigen selects the B-cells that already fit it; it does not instruct any cell to change its antibody.
items.specStatementText: Lymphocytes cooperate to make antibodies
items.random_wrong: Helper T-cells and B-lymphocytes both secrete antibodies, which is why they are said to cooperate in producing them.

items.q: Which statement about antigens is correct?
items.correct: Most antigens are glycoproteins or other proteins, usually located on the outer surface of a pathogen.
items.misconception: Antigens are proteins made by lymphocytes that bind to pathogens and mark them for destruction by the phagocytes.
items.why: The words antigen and antibody are met together, look alike, and both begin with 'anti-', which in everyday language means 'against'. An antigen triggers antibody production; an antibody is produced by B-lymphocytes and binds to the antigen. The antigen belongs to the pathogen (or to a foreign cell), not to the immune system.
items.specStatementText: Antigens are the foreign molecules that trigger the response
items.random_wrong: Antigens are toxins released by a pathogen into the blood, and it is these toxins that the antibodies must neutralize.

items.q: In an experiment, B-lymphocytes specific to an antigen were cultured with that antigen and no other cells. No antibody was produced. When helper T-lymphocytes were added to the culture, antibody production began. What does this show?
items.correct: A B-lymphocyte is activated to produce antibodies only when it both binds its specific antigen and makes contact with a helper T-lymphocyte.
items.misconception: The antibody in the second culture was secreted by the helper T-lymphocytes, which make antibody when they meet an antigen.
items.why: The statement that lymphocytes 'cooperate to produce antibodies' is read as meaning both types make them, and the two lymphocyte types are hard to tell apart. Lymphocytes cooperate in that helper T-cells activate B-cells, but antibody production is carried out only by B-cells, which divide to form clones of antibody-secreting plasma cells.
items.specStatementText: Helper T-cells switch B-cells on
items.random_wrong: Binding of the antigen alone should have activated the B-lymphocytes, so the first culture must have been set up incorrectly.

items.q: Which statement about the transmission of HIV is correct?
items.correct: HIV is transmitted in body fluids such as blood, semen, vaginal secretions and breast milk, for example through unprotected sex, shared needles or from mother to child.
items.misconception: HIV is transmitted through the air by coughing, and by casual contact such as shaking hands, sharing cutlery or using the same toilet as an infected person.
items.why: Students generalize from airborne and contact diseases such as colds, and stigma around HIV reinforces the idea that any contact is dangerous. HIV is transmitted in body fluids. It is not transmitted through the air, by touch, by saliva or by sharing objects, because the virus does not survive outside the body and is not present in those fluids in sufficient amounts.
items.specStatementText: HIV passes only in certain body fluids
items.random_wrong: HIV is transmitted by blood-feeding insects such as mosquitoes, in the same way as the virus that causes Japanese encephalitis is transmitted.

items.q: A person with untreated HIV infection eventually becomes unable to produce antibodies against new pathogens, even though tests show that B-lymphocytes are still present in their blood in substantial numbers. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: HIV infects and kills helper T-lymphocytes, and without contact with an activated helper T-cell a B-lymphocyte cannot be activated to make antibodies.
items.misconception: HIV infects and kills the B-lymphocytes that make the antibodies, so the cells that are needed for antibody production are no longer present in the blood.
items.why: Students reason backwards from the loss of antibody production to the cell that makes antibodies, without considering the activation step. Only certain types of lymphocyte are infected and killed by HIV, principally helper T-cells. Because B-cell activation requires contact with an activated helper T-cell, the reduction in helper T-cells limits the ability to produce antibodies.
items.specStatementText: HIV kills helper T-cells, and AIDS follows
items.random_wrong: Antibodies are secreted by the helper T-lymphocytes, so when HIV destroys these cells the production of all antibodies stops.

items.q: Two people infected with HIV were compared. Person X had 900 helper T-lymphocytes per mm³ of blood and no other infections. Person Y had 150 helper T-lymphocytes per mm³ and had developed pneumonia caused by a fungus that rarely causes disease in healthy people. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: Person Y's loss of helper T-lymphocytes has limited antibody production and defence against infection, so an opportunistic infection has taken hold.
items.misconception: The pneumonia in person Y is caused directly by HIV, which has spread from the blood into the lungs as the infection has progressed.
items.why: AIDS is named and discussed as if it were a single disease, and the idea of one infection allowing others in is unfamiliar. A reduction in helper T-lymphocytes limits the ability to produce antibodies and to fight opportunistic infections. The illnesses of AIDS are caused by other pathogens taking advantage of the weakened immune system.
items.specStatementText: HIV kills helper T-cells, and AIDS follows
items.random_wrong: Person Y's B-lymphocytes have all been destroyed by HIV, which is why antibodies against the fungus have not been produced.

items.q: Why do antibiotics fail to control infections caused by viruses?
items.correct: Viruses have no metabolic processes of their own; they use those of the host cell, which antibiotics do not block.
items.misconception: Viruses are far smaller than bacteria, so antibiotic molecules are too large to bind to them or to enter them effectively.
items.why: Size and living inside cells are the two facts about viruses that students remember best, so they are offered as the explanation. The reason is biochemical, not physical. An antibiotic works by blocking a specific bacterial process, such as cell wall synthesis; a virus has no such process to block, whatever its size or location.
items.specStatementText: Antibiotics hit bacterial processes, which viruses do not have
items.random_wrong: Antibiotics would destroy the human cells inside which viruses replicate, so they cannot safely be used against a viral infection.

items.q: Penicillin blocks the enzymes that build cross-links in the peptidoglycan cell wall of bacteria. A patient takes penicillin for a bacterial infection. Why does the drug kill the bacteria without harming the patient's own cells?
items.correct: Human cells have no cell wall and do not synthesize peptidoglycan, so the process that penicillin blocks does not occur in the patient's cells at all.
items.misconception: Penicillin does damage the patient's cells in the same way, but the patient has so many more cells that the loss is not noticeable.
items.why: Side effects of antibiotics, and the model of chemotherapy damaging all dividing cells, suggest that any drug that kills cells must be indiscriminate. The usefulness of antibiotics depends on their selectivity: they block processes, such as peptidoglycan synthesis or protein synthesis on bacterial ribosomes, that do not occur in eukaryotic cells.
items.specStatementText: Antibiotics hit bacterial processes, which viruses do not have
items.random_wrong: Penicillin cannot reach the inside of human cells, so it only acts on bacteria, which live outside cells in the blood and tissues.

items.q: A hospital ward uses one particular antibiotic heavily. Over several years, an increasing proportion of the bacteria isolated from patients on the ward are found to be resistant to it. Which statement correctly explains this change?
items.correct: Random mutations had given a few bacteria resistance; the antibiotic killed the susceptible ones, so resistant bacteria survived, reproduced and became more common.
items.misconception: Repeated exposure to the antibiotic caused individual bacteria to develop resistance during their own lifetimes, and they passed on this acquired trait to their offspring.
items.why: The phrase 'bacteria become resistant' suggests a response by the organism, and students know that people build up tolerance to drugs with repeated use. Resistance evolves by natural selection. The mutation that confers resistance arises randomly and is present before exposure; the antibiotic does not create it but selects for it by killing the bacteria that lack it.
items.specStatementText: Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
items.random_wrong: The patients on the ward gradually became resistant to the antibiotic, so it stopped working against the bacteria that were infecting them.

items.q: Researchers screened a chemical library of thousands of compounds using a computer model trained to predict antibacterial activity. They identified a compound, structurally unlike any existing antibiotic, that killed several multiresistant strains of bacteria in the laboratory. Which statement is the best evaluation of this work?
items.correct: A new technique has opened a new avenue of research; the compound still needs testing, and careful use of antibiotics is still necessary.
items.misconception: Because the compound kills multiresistant strains, bacteria will not be able to evolve resistance to it, since they have not previously encountered it.
items.why: Resistance is imagined as a reaction to a drug's history rather than as the selection of random variants, so a drug with no history seems immune to it. Resistance arises by random mutation and selection, and mutations conferring resistance can exist before a drug is ever used. New antibiotics found by searching chemical libraries buy time but do not remove the need for careful use.
items.specStatementText: Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
items.random_wrong: Because the results have been published, the compound can be regarded as a proven antibiotic that is ready to be given to patients.

items.q: A farm worker develops tuberculosis after drinking unpasteurized milk from a cow infected with the bacterium Mycobacterium bovis. Which statement about this infection is correct?
items.correct: It is a zoonosis, because the pathogen has transferred from another species of animal to a human.
items.misconception: It is not a zoonosis, because zoonoses are transmitted only by animal bites or by insect vectors, not in food.
items.why: Rabies and mosquito-borne diseases are the best-known animal-linked infections, so their routes are generalized to all zoonoses. Zoonoses reach humans by varied routes, including bites, vectors, contaminated food such as milk, and respiratory droplets. The defining feature is transfer from another species, not the route.
items.specStatementText: Many human diseases come from other animals
items.random_wrong: It is not a zoonosis, because tuberculosis is a human disease that only occasionally infects cattle and other animals.

items.q: Which statement about COVID-19 is correct?
items.correct: It is a zoonosis: SARS-CoV-2 is thought to have transferred to humans from another species recently, and it then spread widely between people.
items.misconception: It is a zoonosis, which means that every case of COVID-19 was caught directly from an infected animal rather than from another person.
items.why: The definition focuses on the animal origin, so students assume the animal must be the source of every case. A zoonosis is an infectious disease that can transfer from other species to humans; whether it then spreads between humans depends on the pathogen. COVID-19 is a zoonosis that became a human pandemic through person-to-person transmission.
items.specStatementText: Many human diseases come from other animals
items.random_wrong: It is not a zoonosis, because SARS-CoV-2 arose within the human population, and diseases only very rarely transfer from animals to humans.

items.q: An mRNA vaccine against COVID-19 contains RNA with the sequence coding for the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, packaged in lipid nanoparticles. Which statement correctly explains how it stimulates immunity?
items.correct: Cells translate the RNA into spike protein, an antigen that stimulates the adaptive immune system to form memory cells without causing disease.
items.misconception: The RNA is translated into antibodies against the spike protein, which then circulate in the blood ready to bind to the virus.
items.why: Antibodies are the molecules associated with protection, and treatments that do inject antibodies (such as antivenom) are known from everyday life. Vaccines contain antigens, or nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) with sequences that code for antigens. They stimulate the development of immunity, which means the formation of the person's own memory cells, rather than supplying antibody directly.
items.specStatementText: Vaccines deliver antigens, not the disease
items.random_wrong: The RNA produces a weakened form of the whole virus inside the person's cells, giving a mild case of COVID-19 that generates immunity.

items.q: For measles, transmission in a population is greatly impeded once about 95% of people are immune. A community's vaccination coverage falls from 96% to 85%. Which statement correctly describes a consequence?
items.correct: People who are not immune, including those who cannot be vaccinated, are at greater risk because chains of transmission are no longer broken.
items.misconception: The unvaccinated people remain immune too, because herd immunity continues to protect the whole population permanently once it has been reached.
items.why: The word 'immunity' is taken literally, as a property each person acquires, rather than as a description of the population. Herd immunity is a property of the population: if a sufficient percentage is immune, transmission is greatly impeded. Individuals who are not immune are shielded by others, not made immune themselves, and lose that protection if coverage falls.
items.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
items.random_wrong: Only the people who chose not to be vaccinated are affected, because each person's vaccination status affects only their own risk of infection.

items.q: A news article reports a newly published study claiming that a vaccine causes a rare side effect, before other scientists have evaluated the study. Which response shows the best understanding of how science works?
items.correct: Treat the claim as provisional until other scientists have evaluated the study; vaccine risks are minimal but not nil.
items.misconception: Accept the claim as established, because a study that has been published in a scientific journal has been proven to be correct.
items.why: News reports say 'scientists have proven', and students have not seen the process of evaluation that follows publication. Publication is the start of evaluation by other scientists, not the end. Consumers of media reports need to be aware that a reported result may still be under evaluation, and that the distinction between pragmatic truths and certainty is poorly understood.
items.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
items.random_wrong: Conclude that the vaccine is unsafe, because a vaccine that is genuinely safe would carry no risk of side effects of any kind.

items.q: In a country, the number of new COVID-19 cases recorded per day fell from 2000 in one week to 1600 in the following week. What is the percentage change in the daily number of cases?
items.correct: Fell by 20%
items.misconception: Fell by 25%
items.why: Students remember 'divide the difference by the value' but not which value, and the final value is the one most recently written down. Percentage change measures the change relative to where the quantity started, so the denominator is always the initial value. Dividing by the final value gives a different, incorrect figure.
items.specStatementText: Percentage change and percentage difference
items.random_wrong: Fell by 22%

items.q: In one week, region P recorded 640 COVID-19 hospital admissions per million people and region Q recorded 960 per million. Taking the mean of the two rates as the reference value, what is the percentage difference between the two regions' admission rates, to the nearest whole number?
items.why: The two terms sound alike and both take the form difference ÷ something × 100, so students treat them as interchangeable and do not check which reference value the question implies. Percentage difference = difference ÷ mean of the two values × 100. Using the mean makes the result symmetrical, which is appropriate when comparing two groups or regions rather than a before and an after.
items.specStatementText: Percentage change and percentage difference

items.q: Is every microorganism that lives on or in the human body a pathogen?
items.correct: No. A pathogen is an organism that causes disease; most of the microorganisms living on the skin and in the gut do not cause disease.
items.misconception: Any microorganism that lives on or inside the body is a pathogen, so all microorganisms are harmful.
items.why: The everyday word 'germs' lumps all microorganisms together as harmful, and examples of microorganisms in early courses are mostly disease examples. Pathogens are the cause of infectious diseases, but only a small fraction of microorganisms are pathogens. The definition depends on causing disease, not on being a microorganism.
items.specStatementText: Pathogens cause infectious disease, and observation beat germ theory to it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the primary defences work by using immune cells or antibodies?
items.correct: No. The skin and mucous membranes are barriers that stop pathogens entering; they do not rely on immune cells or antibodies, which act once a pathogen is inside.
items.misconception: Every defence against pathogens is carried out by immune cells or antibodies, so barriers only work because immune cells or antibodies patrol them.
items.why: The immune system is presented as 'the body's defence', so students assume any defence must involve its cells or its antibodies, and the phrase 'first line of defence' suggests troops rather than a wall. The primary defence is a barrier. The skin's dead outer layer and low-pH surface and the mucus of mucous membranes prevent entry without the involvement of lymphocytes or antibodies; the immune system responds to pathogens that get past these barriers.
items.specStatementText: Skin and mucous membranes stop pathogens getting in
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the secretions of the skin and mucous membranes produced only in response to infection?
items.correct: No. Sebum and mucus are produced continuously, so they form a standing defence that is in place before any pathogen arrives.
items.misconception: Mucus and other secretions are produced only when the body is infected, so they are part of the response to disease rather than a barrier.
items.why: The mucus students notice is the extra produced during a cold, and 'defence' is associated with fighting an infection that has already started. Skin and mucous membranes are primary defences: they are present all the time and act before infection. Mucus continuously traps pathogens on mucous membranes, and sebum continuously keeps the skin surface acidic.
items.specStatementText: Skin and mucous membranes stop pathogens getting in
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a blood clot simply a mass of platelets stuck together?
items.correct: No. Platelets release clotting factors that start a cascade leading to thrombin; thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and it is the fibrin mesh trapping erythrocytes that forms the clot.
items.misconception: The clot is a plug of platelets stuck to each other; no plasma proteins are involved.
items.why: Earlier courses say 'platelets help the blood to clot' without describing what they release, so the platelets themselves are taken to be the clot. Platelets start clotting by releasing clotting factors, but the clot that seals the cut is a mesh of fibrin fibres, produced from fibrinogen by thrombin, in which erythrocytes are trapped.
items.specStatementText: Clotting seals a cut
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is clotting organized as a cascade of steps rather than a single reaction?
items.correct: Each step activates many molecules of the next, so the cascade amplifies the signal from a few clotting factors into the rapid conversion of large amounts of fibrinogen to fibrin.
items.misconception: A cascade of many steps makes clotting slower than a single reaction would be.
items.why: A 'chain of steps' sounds like a delay, and students have not met the idea that enzyme cascades amplify a signal. The cascade is what makes clotting rapid: because each activated enzyme acts on many molecules of the next component, a small initial release of clotting factors quickly produces enough thrombin to convert fibrinogen to fibrin across the whole wound.
items.specStatementText: Clotting seals a cut
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is each phagocyte specific to one type of pathogen?
items.correct: No. Phagocytes are part of the innate system: they recognize broad categories of pathogen and one phagocyte can engulf many different kinds.
items.misconception: Each phagocyte recognizes and destroys only the particular pathogen it is specific to, in the same way as a lymphocyte.
items.why: Specificity is stressed throughout the topic (antibodies, B-cells, helper T-cells), and the guide's phrase 'phagocytes recognize pathogens' is read as meaning specific recognition. Specificity is the property of the adaptive system. The innate system responds to broad categories of pathogen, and phagocytes engulf and digest whatever they recognize as foreign, without being specific to one pathogen.
items.specStatementText: Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: On first exposure to a pathogen, which system responds faster, the innate or the adaptive?
items.correct: The innate system. The adaptive response is specific but takes days to develop on first exposure, because the few specific lymphocytes must be activated and multiply.
items.misconception: The adaptive immune system responds faster than the innate system because a specific response is more efficient.
items.why: Students learn that the adaptive system is 'more effective' and that the secondary response is fast, and assume the better system must also be the quicker one on every occasion. The innate response is immediate but unchanging; the adaptive response is slow on first exposure and becomes fast and effective only on later exposures because of memory cells.
items.specStatementText: Innate is broad and fixed; adaptive is specific and learns
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a phagocyte engulfs a bacterium, does the bacterium enter the cytoplasm?
items.correct: No. The plasma membrane folds around the bacterium and encloses it in a vesicle; the bacterium stays inside the vesicle, separated from the cytoplasm, until it is digested.
items.misconception: Engulfing means the pathogen passes through the plasma membrane straight into the cytoplasm.
items.why: Diagrams show the pathogen 'inside' the phagocyte and students do not yet picture the membrane-bound vesicle formed by endocytosis. Endocytosis encloses the pathogen in a vesicle formed from the plasma membrane. Lysosomes fuse with this vesicle and their enzymes digest the pathogen inside it; the enzymes and the pathogen never mix freely with the cytoplasm.
items.specStatementText: Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are lymphocytes found?
items.correct: They circulate in the blood and are also contained in lymph nodes, which are on the lymph vessels that drain the tissues.
items.misconception: Lymphocytes are found only in the blood; lymph nodes are just filters that trap pathogens.
items.why: Lymphocytes are named as white blood cells, and lymph nodes are only encountered as 'swollen glands'. Lymphocytes both circulate in the blood and are contained in lymph nodes. Lymph nodes swell during infection because lymphocytes there are multiplying.
items.specStatementText: Lymphocytes cooperate to make antibodies
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can molecules on human cells act as antigens?
items.correct: Yes. Antigens on the surface of erythrocytes, for example, stimulate antibody production if the cells are transfused into a person with a different blood group.
items.misconception: Only pathogens carry antigens; human cells have none, so blood from anyone can be transfused into anyone.
items.why: Antigens are introduced as 'markers on the surface of a pathogen', so students define them by their source rather than by the response they provoke. An antigen is any molecule recognized as foreign that triggers antibody production. Erythrocytes carry surface antigens that differ between blood groups, which is why donor and recipient must be matched.
items.specStatementText: Antigens are the foreign molecules that trigger the response
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What kind of molecule is an antigen, and where is it found?
items.correct: Most antigens are glycoproteins or other proteins, and they are usually located on the outer surface of the pathogen.
items.misconception: An antigen is a toxin that a pathogen releases into the blood.
items.why: Toxins are taught as the way bacteria make people ill, and 'antigen' sounds like something that generates harm, so the two ideas merge. Antigens are recognition molecules, usually surface glycoproteins or other proteins, not secreted poisons. A pathogen is recognized by the antigens on its outer surface whether or not it produces a toxin.
items.specStatementText: Antigens are the foreign molecules that trigger the response
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can any helper T-lymphocyte activate any B-lymphocyte?
items.correct: No. Both are antigen-specific: the helper T-cell must have been activated by the same type of antigen as the B-cell it activates.
items.misconception: Helper T-cells are general helpers, so any activated helper T-cell can switch on any B-cell it meets.
items.why: The word 'helper' suggests a non-specific supporting role, and the specificity taught for B-cells is not extended to T-cells. There are antigen-specific B-cells and antigen-specific helper T-cells. A B-cell is activated only by contact with a helper T-cell that has itself become activated by the same type of antigen.
items.specStatementText: Helper T-cells switch B-cells on
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the plasma cells in a clone make different antibodies?
items.correct: No. A clone is produced by mitosis, so all its cells are genetically identical and every plasma cell in it makes the same type of antibody.
items.misconception: The clone of plasma cells makes a range of different antibodies so that the pathogen is attacked in several ways.
items.why: In everyday use 'a range of weapons' seems better than one, and students do not connect the word clone with the identical products of mitosis. Activated B-cells divide by mitosis to produce a clone of plasma cells that are all capable of producing the same type of antibody, the one that fits the antigen that activated the original cell.
items.specStatementText: Activated B-cells multiply into a clone of plasma cells
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do memory cells secrete antibodies continuously?
items.correct: No. Memory cells persist without secreting antibody; when the antigen reappears they divide rapidly to form plasma cells, which secrete it.
items.misconception: Memory cells are plasma cells that keep making the antibody at a low rate for years.
items.why: The word 'memory' is attached to the antibody rather than to the cell, and a cell that 'remembers how to make' the antibody is assumed to be making it. Memory cells are long-lived lymphocytes that are capable of making the specific antibody. They respond to a second exposure by dividing to form plasma cells, so antibody appears faster and in greater quantity than on first exposure.
items.specStatementText: Memory cells are why immunity lasts
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can mosquitoes transmit HIV?
items.correct: No. HIV is not transmitted by insects; it is transmitted in blood, semen, vaginal secretions and breast milk passed directly between people.
items.misconception: HIV is spread by blood-feeding insects such as mosquitoes, in the same way as other viruses found in blood.
items.why: Students learn that malaria and Japanese encephalitis are carried by mosquitoes and know that HIV is present in blood, so the routes are merged. The mechanisms of HIV transmission are unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing of needles, transfusion of unscreened blood and mother-to-child transmission. HIV does not replicate in mosquitoes and is not transmitted by their bites.
items.specStatementText: HIV passes only in certain body fluids
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is having HIV the same as having AIDS?
items.correct: No. HIV is the virus; AIDS is the syndrome that develops, often years later, when HIV has killed so many helper T-cells that the immune system can no longer control opportunistic infections.
items.misconception: HIV is just another name for AIDS, so anyone infected with HIV has AIDS.
items.why: The two are usually written together as 'HIV/AIDS' in the media, and students have not met the idea of a long symptom-free period of infection. Infection of lymphocytes by HIV has AIDS as a consequence, but not immediately. A person with HIV is infectious from the start, and AIDS is diagnosed only when the reduction in helper T-cells has led to failure of antibody production and opportunistic infections.
items.specStatementText: HIV kills helper T-cells, and AIDS follows
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does HIV destroy every type of white blood cell?
items.correct: No. Only certain types of lymphocyte are infected and killed, principally helper T-lymphocytes; phagocytes and B-lymphocytes are not destroyed by the virus.
items.misconception: HIV infects and destroys all white blood cells, so the whole immune system is wiped out.
items.why: AIDS is described as 'the immune system failing', so students picture all the immune cells being killed rather than one type being lost. HIV infects only certain lymphocytes. The loss of helper T-cells is enough to cripple antibody production, because B-cells cannot be activated without them, even though the other cells remain.
items.specStatementText: HIV kills helper T-cells, and AIDS follows
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can antibiotics cure viral infections such as colds and influenza?
items.correct: No. Antibiotics block processes that occur in bacteria; viruses have no such processes of their own, so antibiotics have no effect on them.
items.misconception: Antibiotics are general anti-infection drugs, so they work against viral infections as well as bacterial ones.
items.why: Antibiotics are sometimes prescribed during viral illnesses to treat secondary bacterial infections, and the name 'anti-biotic' sounds as if it means 'against living things' in general. Antibiotics are chemicals that block processes occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells. Viruses reproduce using the host cell's metabolism, which antibiotics do not block, so they fail to control viral infections.
items.specStatementText: Antibiotics hit bacterial processes, which viruses do not have
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Who or what becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
items.correct: The strain of bacteria, not the patient. Resistance is a heritable property of the bacterial population.
items.misconception: People who take antibiotics too often become resistant to them, so the drugs stop working on that person.
items.why: The phrase 'antibiotic resistance' is heard in public health messages about personal overuse, and 'resistance' sounds like something the body builds. Antibiotic resistance is a property of strains of pathogenic bacteria that have evolved it. Overuse matters because it increases the selection pressure on bacterial populations, not because it changes the patient.
items.specStatementText: Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a single mutation make a bacterium resistant to all antibiotics?
items.correct: No. Each antibiotic blocks a different process, so resistance to each requires its own mutation or gene; multiresistant strains have accumulated several.
items.misconception: A single mutation makes a bacterium tougher in general, so it becomes resistant to all antibiotics at once.
items.why: The word 'superbug' suggests a generally hardier organism rather than one that has collected several specific resistance genes. Strains evolve resistance to several antibiotics by accumulating separate resistance genes, often under selection by several drugs in turn. Careful use of antibiotics is needed to slow the emergence of multiresistant bacteria.
items.specStatementText: Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the discovery of new antibiotics remove the need to use existing ones carefully?
items.correct: No. Every antibiotic selects for resistance when it is used, so careful use is needed to slow the emergence of multiresistant bacteria whatever new drugs are found.
items.misconception: As long as new antibiotics keep being discovered, there is no need to limit the use of existing ones.
items.why: Discovery is reported as a solution to resistance, and the slow, expensive process of bringing a drug into use is invisible to students. Careful use of antibiotics is necessary to slow the emergence of multiresistant bacteria. New techniques such as searching chemical libraries are yielding new antibiotics, but resistance to those will also evolve if they are used carelessly.
items.specStatementText: Resistance evolves by natural selection, so use antibiotics carefully
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are zoonoses a rare category of human disease?
items.correct: No. A large proportion of human infectious diseases, and most newly emerging ones, originated in other species.
items.misconception: Zoonoses are rare curiosities; most human infectious diseases arose in humans.
items.why: The familiar diseases (colds, measles, influenza) feel purely human, and their animal origins are not part of how they are taught. Zoonoses are prevalent among human infectious diseases and their modes of infection are varied: tuberculosis (from cattle), rabies (from bites), Japanese encephalitis (via mosquitoes from pigs and birds) and COVID-19 (recently from another species) are all zoonoses.
items.specStatementText: Many human diseases come from other animals
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all zoonoses caused by viruses?
items.correct: No. Tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium bovis is a bacterial zoonosis; rabies, Japanese encephalitis and COVID-19 are viral.
items.misconception: Only viruses can cross from one species to another, so all zoonoses are viral.
items.why: The zoonoses in the news (COVID-19, bird flu, rabies) are viral, and bacteria are thought of as living in one host. Zoonoses include bacterial and other pathogens as well as viruses. Tuberculosis is among the examples the IB names, and its bovine form is transmitted from cattle to humans in unpasteurized milk.
items.specStatementText: Many human diseases come from other animals
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a vaccine give a person a mild case of the disease?
items.correct: No. A vaccine stimulates immunity to a specific pathogen without causing the disease; any mild symptoms come from the immune response, not from the disease.
items.misconception: A vaccine gives you a mild dose of the disease so that you can fight the real one later.
items.why: Vaccines are described as containing a 'weakened' pathogen, and people sometimes feel unwell for a day after vaccination. Vaccines contain antigens or nucleic acid coding for antigens, not a functioning pathogen able to cause the disease. The antigens trigger the adaptive response, including memory cells, without the disease occurring.
items.specStatementText: Vaccines deliver antigens, not the disease
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an mRNA vaccine change a person's DNA?
items.correct: No. The mRNA is translated by ribosomes in the cytoplasm into the antigen protein and is then broken down; it does not enter the nucleus or become part of the person's DNA.
items.misconception: An mRNA vaccine inserts genetic material into a person's chromosomes, permanently changing their genes.
items.why: The vaccine is described as 'genetic', and students blur the distinction between DNA and RNA and between translation and integration into a genome. The nucleic acid in a vaccine carries a sequence coding for an antigen. In an mRNA vaccine the RNA is translated in the cytoplasm to produce the antigen for a short time; the person's own genome is not altered.
items.specStatementText: Vaccines deliver antigens, not the disease
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a person's decision to be vaccinated affect anyone other than themselves?
items.correct: Yes. Members of a population are interdependent: each immune person reduces transmission, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated or who did not respond to a vaccine.
items.misconception: Whether or not I am vaccinated affects only my own risk of catching the disease.
items.why: Health decisions are framed as personal choices, and the chain of transmission through other people is not visible. Members of a population are interdependent in building herd immunity. A person who is vaccinated cannot pass the disease on, so their choice reduces the risk to others, including infants and people with weakened immune systems.
items.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Once herd immunity has been reached, has the disease been removed for good?
items.correct: No. Herd immunity only impedes transmission while the immune percentage stays high; if vaccination coverage falls, the disease can return and epidemics can occur.
items.misconception: Once herd immunity is achieved, the pathogen is gone for good, so a later fall in vaccination coverage does not matter.
items.why: Diseases that are no longer seen locally feel like they have been eliminated, and the ongoing need for vaccination is invisible. Herd immunity prevents epidemics only as long as a sufficient percentage of the population is immune. Measles outbreaks in communities where coverage has fallen show that the protection is conditional.
items.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a vaccine have to be risk-free to be considered safe?
items.correct: No. Vaccines are tested rigorously and the risk of side effects is minimal but not nil; safe means that the small risk is far outweighed by the benefit.
items.misconception: A safe vaccine must have no risk of side effects at all; any reported side effect shows that the vaccine is unsafe.
items.why: Safety is treated as an absolute rather than a comparison of risks, and any reported harm is taken as disproof. The risks of side effects from vaccines are minimal but not nil. Recognizing that a claim can be reliable enough to act on without being certain is part of understanding pragmatic truth in science.
items.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Because vaccines are tested rigorously, is it certain that a given vaccine has no side effects?
items.correct: No. Rigorous testing makes serious side effects very unlikely, but science provides pragmatic truths rather than certainty, and rare effects may only be detected after widespread use.
items.misconception: Rigorous testing means a vaccine is certain to be free of side effects, so any claim of a side effect can be dismissed without looking at it.
items.why: Rigorous testing is presented as a guarantee, and students confuse 'very well supported' with 'certain'. Scientific claims are pragmatic truths: reliable enough to act on but open to revision. A new claim about a rare side effect should be evaluated on its evidence, neither accepted on publication nor dismissed because of prior testing.
items.specStatementText: Herd immunity protects those who cannot be vaccinated
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If daily cases fall from 2000 to 1600, is the percentage change 80%?
items.correct: No. 1600 ÷ 2000 × 100 = 80% is the final value as a percentage of the initial value; the change is 80% − 100% = −20%.
items.misconception: Dividing the new value by the old value and multiplying by 100 gives the percentage change directly.
items.why: Students compute 'new as a percentage of old', which is a familiar calculation, and report it without subtracting 100%. Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100. The ratio of final to initial is a related quantity but must have 100% subtracted from it to give the change.
items.specStatementText: Percentage change and percentage difference
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the percentage difference formula, is the denominator the sum of the two values?
items.correct: No. The denominator is the mean of the two values, which is their sum divided by 2.
items.misconception: Percentage difference is the difference divided by the sum of the two values, multiplied by 100.
items.why: The formula is remembered as having '(a + b)' in the denominator, and the division by 2 that turns the sum into a mean is dropped. Percentage difference = |a − b| ÷ ((a + b) ÷ 2) × 100. Dividing by the sum instead of the mean gives an answer exactly half the correct one.
items.specStatementText: Percentage change and percentage difference
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
